articles.title: How to read a job ad

body.support:
Most job ads have **six parts**.

1. **The role.** The job and if it's **casual**. Casual means no set hours.
2. **The pay.** *Award rates* means the lowest pay the law allows. **Super** is money saved for when you retire.
3. **The hours.** When they need you.
4. **Essential.** What you **must** have.
5. **Desirable.** What would **help**. You can still apply.
6. **How to apply.** What to send, where, and by when.

Some words have a hidden meaning. *Fast-paced* means busy.

Watch for **fake ads**. Big pay for easy work? A chat app? Paying to start? It's a scam. A real boss pays **you**.
body.core:
Job ads look different, but nearly all have the same **six parts**. Learn where to find them and you can read an ad in a minute.

1. **The role.** The job title and the kind of work: **casual**, part-time or full-time. Casual means no set hours. You're usually paid a bit more per hour, but you don't get paid holidays or sick days.
2. **The pay.** It might be a dollar amount, or **award rates + super**. An **award rate** is the lowest pay the law allows for that job. **Super** is money your employer saves for you for when you retire.
3. **The hours.** When they need you. If the ad says *weekends only* and you play footy on Saturdays, it's not for you.
4. **Essential.** What you **must** have: maybe being 15 or over, a Working with Children Check, or being able to work Saturday mornings.
5. **Desirable.** What would **help**: experience, a food handling certificate. You can still apply without these.
6. **How to apply.** What to send (a resume, a short message), where to send it, and the **closing date**.

Job ads also use **code words**. *Fast-paced* means busy. *Flexible availability* means they might call you in at short notice. *Team player* means you'll work closely with others. Reading between the lines tells you what the job is really like.

Finally, watch for **scams**. Fake job ads promise big pay for easy work, move you to chat apps like WhatsApp, or ask you to pay money to start. A real employer pays you, not the other way around.

And know your rights: an unpaid **trial** is only allowed if it's short, supervised and just to show your skills. If you're doing real work, you should be paid.
body.extend:
Job ads vary in style, but most share **six parts**. Knowing them lets you find key information fast.

1. **The role**: title and type of work. **Casual** work has no set hours. Casuals are usually paid a higher hourly rate instead of paid leave.
2. **The pay**: a figure, or **award rates + super**. The **award** sets the legal minimum for the job. **Super** is what your employer pays into your retirement savings.
3. **The hours**: when you'll be needed.
4. **Essential criteria**: non-negotiable requirements, such as a minimum age, a Working with Children Check or specific availability.
5. **Desirable criteria**: advantages, not requirements. Don't talk yourself out of applying because you don't meet them all.
6. **How to apply**: documents, method and **closing date**.

Ads also use stock phrases that soften the truth. *Fast-paced environment* signals pressure. *Flexible availability* can mean shifts at short notice. *Competitive pay* tells you nothing specific. Inferring what's implied is part of reading the ad.

Finally, judge reliability. Scam ads offer unusually high pay for simple tasks, move contact to messaging apps, or ask for payment to start. Under Fair Work rules, an unpaid trial must be short, supervised and only to show skills. Real work must be paid.

caseStudies.title: The job that cost money

body.support:
Fake job ads are a big problem. In **2024**, people in Australia lost **$13.7 million** to job scams.

Young people are often the target. Students looking for part-time work are hit hard.

Here's how it works. A “boss” messages you on an app. They offer good money for easy tasks, like liking videos. Then they say you have to **pay** to earn more. You never get the money back.

The government took down more than **1,850 fake job ads** in six months.

The warning signs: pay that's too good, jobs that are too easy, chat apps, and being asked to **pay**.
body.core:
Job scams are one of the fastest-growing scams in Australia. In **2023**, Australians reported losing **$24.3 million** to them, up **151%** from the year before. In **2024**, Scamwatch got more than **3,000 reports**, with losses of **$13.7 million**.

Scamwatch says these scams hit people aged **18 to 44** the hardest, including **students looking for part-time work**.

A common trick is the **task scam**. A “recruiter” messages you, often on WhatsApp or social media. They offer good pay for easy online tasks, like rating products or liking videos. At first you might even get a small payment. Then they say you need to pay money to unlock bigger earnings. The money never comes back.

The government's **National Anti-Scam Centre** set up a team to fight job scams. Between **September 2024 and March 2025**, it had more than **1,850 fake job ads** and **29,000 scam social media accounts** taken down.

The warning signs are in the text: pay that's too good, tasks that are too easy, a chat app instead of a real application, and any request for **you** to pay **them**.
body.extend:
Job scams have grown fast in Australia. Reported losses reached **$24.3 million** in **2023**, up **151%** on 2022. In **2024**, Scamwatch received more than **3,000 reports**, with **$13.7 million** lost.

Scamwatch data show these scams disproportionately affect Australians aged **18 to 44**, including **students seeking part-time work**.

The most common type is the **task-based scam**. A fake recruiter, usually on a messaging app or social media, offers generous pay for simple online tasks. Small early payments build trust. Then victims are told to deposit money to unlock bigger earnings, which never arrive.

In response, the **National Anti-Scam Centre** formed a job scam fusion cell. Between **September 2024 and March 2025**, it removed more than **29,000 scam social media accounts** and **1,850 fake job ads**.

The red flags are in the text: pay that's too good, vague or trivial duties, informal contact, and any request for the worker to pay the employer.

teacher.answers:
**Check your reading:** essential = must have; desirable = helps but not required. Award rates = the legal minimum pay for the job; super = money your employer saves for your retirement. Red flags: very high pay for easy tasks, chat apps, paying to start.

**Job ad:** 1 role (casual: no set hours, no paid leave); 2 pay (award minimum + super); 3 hours; 4 essential (fast-paced = busy); 5 desirable; 6 how to apply (closing date; no reply may mean no).

**Read between the lines (samples):** flexible availability — they may call you in at short notice; team player — you'll work closely with others; immediate start — they need someone now; competitive pay — vague, tells you nothing specific; only shortlisted contacted — if you don't hear back, you didn't get to the next step.

**Sort:** $500 a day — red flag; casual award rates — looks real; WhatsApp — red flag; email by Friday — looks real; starter fee — red flag; two-week unpaid trial — red flag.

**Case study:** a fake recruiter offers pay for easy online tasks, may pay a little at first, then asks you to deposit money to earn more, which you never get back; students want flexible, easy work and may be less experienced; don't pay, don't share details, check the business independently, report it to Scamwatch.

ACCC — National Anti-Scam Centre fusion cell on job scams

realityCheck: **Job sites can be blocked or overwhelming.** Have printed ads ready, and choose roles 14–17 year olds can actually get.
**Pay rules are complex.** Keep to the basics (award minimum, casual vs permanent) and point students to the Fair Work Ombudsman's Pay Calculator rather than quoting rates, which change every year.
**Some students already have jobs.** Use them as experts: what did their job ad say, and what was the job really like?
**Scams are personal for some families.** Someone may have been caught. Keep it practical, not judgemental.
**Works in a real class:** yes. It's quick, relevant and leads straight into Build Your Resume and Nail the Interview.
